# How to Ask Duck.ai to Explain Hard Ideas in Plain English (Step by Step)

> **In short:** You can paste a confusing passage into Duck.ai, ask for an everyday comparison, and then ask follow-up questions until it makes sense. The free AI models are enough to start. Duck.ai can be wrong, so check important points with your teacher or the original source.

When a textbook page loses you, the problem is usually not you. The writing may assume you already know a few things. In this guide you will learn how to ask Duck.ai, DuckDuckGo's AI chat feature, to explain the idea using a comparison from daily life, and then how to keep asking questions until it clicks. No experience with AI is needed.

## Before you start

- **A web browser** on a computer, tablet or phone, with an internet connection.
- **Access to Duck.ai.** You can open it directly, or use it from a DuckDuckGo search. Duck.ai is described as private: DuckDuckGo says it anonymizes your chats and does not store your prompts or train on your data.
- **The passage you want explained**, typed or copied. Use a few paragraphs at a time, not a whole chapter.
- **Plans:** the free models are available to everyone. Paid plans, called Plus and Pro, add more advanced models and higher usage limits. You don't need one to follow this guide. For current plan details, check DuckDuckGo's official help center.
- **Time:** about 10 to 15 minutes.

## Step 1 — Open Duck.ai

There are two easy ways in. You can go straight to Duck.ai in your browser, or run a regular DuckDuckGo search and then move to Duck.ai to ask a follow-up question. If you have added the Duck.ai button to your DuckDuckGo browser, you can also use that button to open it. What you should see is a chat screen with an empty message box, usually at the bottom, where you type your questions. Think of it as a study partner who is waiting for your first question.

If the screen looks different, don't worry. Apps change, and your version may be laid out differently. If you can't find the chat area, look for the Duck.ai button or a link inside DuckDuckGo. DuckDuckGo's official help center explains how to add or remove that button and how to hide it on search results pages if you prefer. Those are the exact details to check.

You'll know it worked when you see a message box where you can type a question and send it.

## Step 2 — Paste the confusing passage and ask for an everyday comparison

Copy the paragraph that confuses you, click into the message box, and paste it. Then add a short instruction telling Duck.ai what you want: a plain-English explanation built around a comparison from everyday life. Name your level, too, so the answer matches what you already know. Duck.ai will read your text and write a reply below your message, usually within a few seconds. Replies can be long, so you may need to scroll down to read the whole thing.

Everyday comparisons work well because they connect a new idea to something you already understand, such as a kitchen, a bus schedule or a sports team. If the first comparison doesn't fit, that's normal, and you can ask for a different one in the next step.

💬 Example: "Explain this passage in plain English, using an everyday comparison a high school student would understand: [paste the paragraph here]"

You'll know it worked when a reply appears below your message and it uses a comparison from daily life to describe the idea.

## Step 3 — Ask follow-up questions until the idea clicks

This is where the real learning happens. Pick the part of the comparison that still feels fuzzy and ask about just that part. Keep your questions short and specific. You can also ask Duck.ai to connect the comparison back to the original passage, so you can see which piece of the comparison matches which part of the textbook. If an answer misses the point, don't give up. Tell it what confused you and try again.

Duck.ai usually keeps the earlier messages in the same conversation, so you can build on them. If it seems to forget something, restate the key detail in your next message. Each AI model answers in its own way, so a rephrased question can sometimes lead to a clearer explanation.

💬 Example: "In your comparison, what part stands for the main idea in the passage? Explain it again in one sentence I could say out loud."

You'll know it worked when you can explain the idea back in your own words, without looking at the reply.

## Step 4 — Check your understanding and come back later

Once the idea makes sense, ask Duck.ai to test you. Request three practice questions based on the passage, answer them yourself, and then ask for feedback. This turns a passive reading session into real practice. When you finish, you can return to the conversation later. Duck.ai's Recent Chats feature keeps your past conversations so you can find them again. According to DuckDuckGo, these chats are stored locally on your device rather than on its servers. You can also pin up to five chats to the top of the list for quick access. Pinning also keeps a chat from being removed by the Fire Button, which is covered in the next step.

If you don't see Recent Chats, look for a history or past-conversations area in the Duck.ai screen. The help center has the current location.

💬 Example: "Quiz me with three questions about this passage, one at a time. Wait for my answer before you tell me if I'm right."

You'll know it worked when your past chat appears in your recent chats list, and you can open it again later to continue studying.

## Step 5 — Clear your chats when you're done

Chats you don't need can be deleted one at a time, or all at once with the Fire Button. DuckDuckGo says the Fire Button clears recent chats, so only use it when you're ready to lose the ones you haven't pinned. Before you delete anything, make sure you have saved what you need, such as a summary or your notes. The official help center describes the exact steps for each option.

Also remember what Duck.ai cannot do. It can explain a passage, but it can't confirm that its explanation matches your exact course, and AI models can make mistakes. If a fact matters for a test or a grade, check it against your textbook or ask your teacher.

💬 Example: "Summarize our conversation in five bullet points I can copy into my study notes."

You'll know it worked when your study notes contain a summary you wrote or copied, and you have decided which chats to keep before you delete anything.

## Common mistakes

- **Pasting too much at once.** A whole chapter makes the answer vague. Fix it by pasting one or two paragraphs, then asking for the next section after you understand the first.
- **Accepting the first explanation without questions.** A comparison can sound clear but still miss a key detail. Fix it by asking "What is this comparison missing?" or asking for one example where it would not work.
- **Deleting chats too quickly.** The Fire Button clears chats you haven't pinned. Fix it by pinning the conversations you want to keep, and copying any notes you need before you clear anything.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** Use this method when you read a manual, a news explainer or a letter about a bill you don't understand. Ask for a comparison, then ask one follow-up.
- **For your business or work:** Paste a dense internal report or training document and ask for a plain-English version you can share with a new team member. Check the facts against the original first.
- **If you're just getting started:** Begin with one short paragraph you already partly understand. Ask for a comparison, then ask one follow-up question. That single exchange is enough to see how the method works.

## Try it now

Pick one paragraph from a textbook, article or manual that has confused you this week. Open Duck.ai, paste the paragraph, and type: "Explain this in plain English with an everyday comparison: [paste the paragraph here]." Then ask one follow-up question about the part you still don't get.
